title: Filesystem and file operations
goal: Move around Linux folders with confidence and create, copy, move, link and delete files safely.
setup: # P1: a small to-do app project
for d in 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09; do echo "log $d" > wild/logs/app-2026-10-$d.log; done

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Copy October logs 01-05 and all .conf files into backup/2026-10' 'mkdir backup/2026-10' 'cp logs\app-2026-10-0[1-5].log backup/2026-10/' 'cp configs backup/2026-10/' 'echo "Backup done"' > wild/backup-logs.sh
touch match/api-1.log match/api-2.log match/api-10.log match/web-1.log match/notes.txt

warmup.q: What does the first line `#!/bin/bash` in a script do?
warmup.a: It is the shebang. It tells Linux which program runs the script (here: bash).
A variable with a list of folders, separated by `:`. Bash searches these folders when the user types a command name.
The exit code of the last command. `0` means success. Any other number means an error.

problems.title: Move around a project: paths, cd and hidden files
problems.situation: Every Linux task starts with moving between folders. On a new server, a DevOps engineer must always know where they are, how to go up and down, and how to see hidden files like `.env`. **Goal:** move around the to-do app project with relative and absolute paths, and find its hidden config file.
outcomes: What the **working directory** is (`pwd`).
**Absolute** paths vs **relative** paths.
The special names `.`, `..`, `~` and `-`.
**Hidden files** and `ls -a`.
task: Go into `todo-app/backend` with a **relative** path. Print where you are with `pwd`.
List the files with `ls`. Then list again with `ls -a`. Which file appears only with `-a`?
Go up one level with `cd ..`. Then go into `frontend/public` and print `pwd`.
Go back to the previous folder with `cd -`.
Use an **absolute** path (starts with `/` or `~`) to go to the backend `logs` folder. Print `pwd` and list it.
hints: A relative path starts from the folder the user is in now. An absolute path starts from `/` (the root directory).
Hidden files start with a dot, like `.env`. `ls -a` shows them. `cd -` jumps back to the last folder.
`cd todo-app/backend` then `pwd`, `ls`, `ls -a`, `cd ..`, `cd frontend/public`, `cd -`, `cd ~/bash-practice/day01/todo-app/backend/logs`.

learn.title: One tree of folders
text: Linux has one tree of folders. The top is `/`, the **root directory**. The terminal always stands in one folder: the **working directory**.
`pwd` prints it. `cd` moves to another folder. `ls` lists what is inside.

learn.title: Absolute or relative path
text: An **absolute** path starts with `/` (or `~`), so it works from any folder. A **relative** path starts from the current folder.

head: Path
Kind
Starts at
rows: parent folder / this folder / previous folder (`cd -`)

learn.title: Hidden files, and / vs \
text: A file whose name starts with a dot (`.env`, `.gitignore`) is **hidden**. `ls` skips it; `ls -a` shows it.
Linux paths use `/`. In bash, `\` is an escape character, so a Windows path breaks:
learn.art: cd todo-app\backend   ->  bash sees: cd todo-appbackend   ->  No such file or directory

steps.say: Go into `todo-app/backend` with a **relative** path (no `/` at the start), then print where we are.
List the folder with plain `ls`.
List **all** files with `ls -a`.
steps.after: Now we see `.env`, plus `.` (this folder) and `..` (the parent).

steps.say: Go up one level with `..`.
Go down into `frontend/public` (relative to `todo-app`).
`cd -` jumps back to the previous folder and prints its name.
Use an **absolute** path. It works from anywhere.

explanation.meaning: Print working directory: the full path of the current folder.
Change directory: move into another folder.
List files. `-a` also shows hidden files (names that start with `.`).
Up one level / back to the previous folder.
Short name for the user's home folder: `/home/wicky`.

mistakes: Using a Windows backslash: `cd todo-app\backend` gives `bash: cd: todo-appbackend: No such file or directory`. Linux paths use `/` (forward slash). The `\` is an escape character in bash, so it disappears.
Forgetting that `ls` hides dot files. The user thinks `.env` is missing, but it is only hidden.
Typing `cd/home` (no space) gives `bash: cd/home: No such file or directory`.

checks.expect: bash: cd: todo-appbackend: No such file or directory
bash: cd/home: No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: An absolute path starts from the root directory `/`, so it works from anywhere. A relative path starts from the current folder. Files whose names start with a dot are hidden; `ls -a` shows them.
problems.try_yourself: Run `cd` with nothing after it, then `pwd`. Where are you? Then try `cd ~-` and see what happens.

problems.title: The Linux folder map: where configs, logs and programs live
problems.situation: Interviewers often ask: "Nginx is broken. Where is its config? Where is its log?" Every Linux server uses the same main folders, so one map works everywhere. **Goal:** check the main folders under `/` and learn what each one is for.
outcomes: What `/etc`, `/var/log`, `/home`, `/tmp`, `/usr/bin`, `/opt` and `/proc` are for.
The root directory `/` vs the root user's home `/root`.
How to find where a command lives.
task: Run `ls /` and look at the top folders. (Your list can be a little different from another machine.)
Run `stat -c '%n -> %F' /etc /var/log /home /tmp /usr/bin /opt /proc` to check that each one is a directory.
Find where the `ls` program lives with `command -v ls`.
Show the owner of `/` (root directory) and of `/root` (home of the root user) with `stat -c '%n owner=%U' / /root`.
Read the first line of `/proc/self/status`. (`/proc` shows live information about running processes.)
hints: Configs live in one folder, logs in another, programs in another. Think: e = etc = settings.
`stat -c` prints only the fields the user asks for. `%n` = name, `%F` = file type, `%U` = owner.
`head -n 1 /proc/self/status` shows the name of the process that reads the file.

learn.title: The map
text: Learn this map. It is the same on every server.
art: ├── root        home of the root user (admin)
├── tmp         temporary, can be deleted at restart
└── proc        LIVE kernel info, not on disk
learn.after: Memory trick: **etc** = settings, **var** = varies (logs grow), **bin** = binaries (programs).

learn.title: Two kinds of "root"
text: `/` is the **root directory**, the top of the tree. `root` is the **admin user**; its home folder is `/root`. They are different things.

steps.say: Look at the top folders. The list is a little different on each machine, so no output is shown.
Check that each main folder is a directory (`%n` = name, `%F` = type).
steps.out:
/etc -> directory
/var/log -> directory
/home -> directory
/tmp -> directory
/usr/bin -> directory
/opt -> directory
/proc -> directory

steps.say: Ask bash where the `ls` program lives.
steps.after: A command is just a program file in a folder like `/usr/bin`.

steps.say: Compare the root directory `/` and the root user's home `/root`.
steps.after: Both belong to the user `root`, but they are two different folders.

steps.say: Read a live file from `/proc`. The kernel makes it at the moment it is read.
steps.after: `self` is the process that reads it, so the name is `head`.

explanation.meaning: Configuration files. Example: `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`, `/etc/hosts`.
Log files. Example: `/var/log/nginx/error.log`, `/var/log/syslog`.
Home folders of normal users. Example: `/home/wicky`.
Temporary files. Often cleaned when the machine restarts.
Programs (commands) installed by the system, like `ls` and `grep`.
Optional or third-party software, for example a Jenkins or a vendor tool.
Not real files on disk. Live information from the kernel about processes, CPU and memory.
`/` is the root directory (top of all folders). `/root` is the home folder of the root user. Two different things.

problems.expected_output:
/etc -> directory
/var/log -> directory
/home -> directory
/tmp -> directory
/usr/bin -> directory
/opt -> directory
/proc -> directory
/usr/bin/ls
/ owner=root
/root owner=root
Name:	head
mistakes: Mixing up `/` (root directory) and `root` (the admin user). The root user's home is `/root`, not `/`.
Looking for logs in `/etc`. Configs are in `/etc`; logs are in `/var/log`.
Thinking `/tmp` is safe storage. Files there can disappear after a restart.
problems.interview_say: Configs are in `/etc`, logs in `/var/log`, user homes in `/home`, temporary files in `/tmp`, programs in `/usr/bin`, and `/proc` shows live process information from the kernel.
problems.try_yourself: Run `ls /proc | head` and `cat /proc/loadavg`. What do you think the numbers in `loadavg` mean? (Day 17 explains them.)

problems.title: Write a script: prepare a release folder
problems.situation: A deploy repeats the same folder steps every time. Typing them by hand is slow and easy to get wrong, so DevOps teams put them in a script. **Goal:** write your first bash script, `prepare-release.sh`. It prepares the folders for release v1.2 and deletes the old release v1.0.
outcomes: How to write, check and run a bash script.
The DevOps script standard: shebang, comments, `set -euo pipefail`, quoted variables.
`mkdir -p` with braces, `touch`, `cp -r`, `mv` and `rm -r`.
How `set -e` stops a script at the first error.
spec: Start with the shebang `#!/bin/bash` and the safety line `set -euo pipefail`.
Keep the release folders in two variables: `NEW="releases/v1.2"` and `OLD="releases/v1.0"`.
Copy both `config` folders from the old release into the new one.
Rename `app.yml` to `app-prod.yml` in the new backend config.
Delete the old release, then print the folder tree.
task: In `day01`, open a new file with `nano prepare-release.sh` and write the script from the list above.
Check it with `bash -n prepare-release.sh` and `shellcheck prepare-release.sh`.
Make it executable with `chmod +x`, then run it with `./prepare-release.sh`.
Run it a second time. What happens, and why?
hints: Start with `#!/bin/bash`, then `set -euo pipefail`, then the two variables. No spaces around `=`.
Write `"$NEW"/{frontend,backend}/logs`: the braces stay outside the quotes. Folders need `cp -r`.
The commands, in order: `mkdir -p`, `touch`, `cp -r` (two times), `mv`, `rm -r`, `tree releases`.

learn.title: A script is a file of commands
text: Bash reads the file from top to bottom and runs each line. Lines that start with `#` are comments; bash ignores them.
Two ways to run it: `bash prepare-release.sh`, or make it executable once (`chmod +x`) and run `./prepare-release.sh`. The `./` means "the file in this folder".

learn.title: The DevOps script standard
text: Start every script like this. Interviewers look for it.

head: Line
Why
rows: The **shebang**: Linux runs the file with bash.
Comments at the top: what it does and how to run it.
Stop at the first error (`-e`), at an unset variable (`-u`), and when any part of a pipe fails.
A **variable**: a name for a value. No spaces around `=`.
Use it with `$` and **double quotes**, so a space in a name cannot break the command.

learn.after: Before running: `bash -n file.sh` checks the syntax, and `shellcheck file.sh` finds common bugs.

learn.title: The file commands in this script

head: Command
What it does
rows: Makes `a/x/logs` and `a/y/logs`, with all missing parents. No error if they exist.
Copies a folder and everything inside it into `DEST`.
Deletes a folder and everything inside. No recycle bin.

files.name: prepare-release.sh
files.say: The finished script. The comments say what each part does and why.
content: #   1. Makes the log folders for the new release (frontend and backend).
#   2. Makes an empty backend log file.
#   3. Copies the config folders from the old release into the new one.
#   4. Renames the backend config to app-prod.yml.
# Safety: stop at the first error (-e), stop when a variable is not set (-u),
# and let a pipe (cmd1 | cmd2) fail if any part of it fails (-o pipefail).
# The two release folders. For the next release, change only these two lines.
# Use variables as "$NAME": the $ reads the value, the double quotes keep it in one piece.
# 1. Log folders. -p makes missing parent folders, and gives no error if they exist.
#    The braces make two paths: $NEW/frontend/logs and $NEW/backend/logs.
#    The braces must stay OUTSIDE the quotes, or bash does not expand them.
# 2. An empty log file for the backend.
# 3. Copy the config folders. They are folders, so cp needs -r (recursive).
#    The / at the end means "copy INTO this folder".
# 4. Rename: mv in the same folder with a new name.
# 5. Delete the old release. No -f, so rm still reports a problem.

steps.say: Open a new file in the editor and type the script. Save with **Ctrl+O**, **Enter**, and close with **Ctrl+X**.
Check the syntax without running anything. No output means no syntax error.
Let ShellCheck look for common bugs (install it once: `sudo apt install -y shellcheck`). No output means it found nothing.
Make the file executable, then run it with `./`.
steps.after: The tree shows both `logs` folders, the empty `app.log`, both configs and the renamed `app-prod.yml`. `v1.0` is gone.
steps.out:
Preparing releases/v1.2 from releases/v1.0
Done. The new release:
releases
└── v1.2
    ├── backend
    │   ├── config
    │   │   └── app-prod.yml
    │   └── logs
    │       └── app.log
    └── frontend
        ├── config
        │   └── nginx.conf
        └── logs

8 directories, 3 files

steps.say: Run it again. `v1.0` does not exist any more, so a `cp` fails. `set -e` stops the script right there. `||` runs the `echo` only when the script fails, and `$?` is its exit code.
steps.after: The script stopped at the first error and did not print "Done". Without `set -e` it would go on and print "Done" anyway (see problem 5).
steps.out:
Preparing releases/v1.2 from releases/v1.0
cp: cannot stat 'releases/v1.0/frontend/config': No such file or directory
The script stopped. Exit code: 1

explanation.meaning: Shebang: run this file with bash.
Stop at the first error, at an unset variable, and when a pipe fails.
Make a variable. Read it with `"$NEW"`.
Quoted variable + brace expansion = two paths.
Check a script before running it.
Make the file executable, then run it from this folder.

problems.expected_output:
Preparing releases/v1.2 from releases/v1.0
Done. The new release:
releases
└── v1.2
    ├── backend
    │   ├── config
    │   │   └── app-prod.yml
    │   └── logs
    │       └── app.log
    └── frontend
        ├── config
        │   └── nginx.conf
        └── logs

8 directories, 3 files
Preparing releases/v1.2 from releases/v1.0
cp: cannot stat 'releases/v1.0/frontend/config': No such file or directory
The script stopped. Exit code: 1
mistakes: Spaces around `=`: `NEW = "releases/v1.2"` gives `bash: NEW: command not found`. Bash thinks `NEW` is a command.
Running it before `chmod +x` gives `bash: ./prepare-release.sh: Permission denied`. Use `chmod +x` once, or run `bash prepare-release.sh`.
Braces inside the quotes: `mkdir -p "$NEW/{frontend,backend}/logs"` makes one folder really called `{frontend,backend}`.
problems.interview_say: I put repeated steps in a script that starts with `#!/bin/bash` and `set -euo pipefail`, keep names in quoted variables, and check it with `bash -n` and `shellcheck` before I run it.
problems.try_yourself: Change the variables to `NEW="releases/v1.3"` and `OLD="releases/v1.2"` and run the script. Which line fails, and why?

problems.title: Symlinks and hard links: the `current` release pointer
problems.situation: Deploy tools keep each version in its own folder and use a link called `current` for the live version. Nginx uses links too (`sites-enabled`). **Goal:** make symlinks and hard links, see what happens when the original file is deleted, and switch `current` like a real deploy.
outcomes: How Linux stores a file: **name** -> **inode** -> **data**.
A **hard link** (second name) vs a **symlink** (a stored path).
Which link survives when the original is deleted.
How `ln -sfn` switches a release in one step.
task: In `links`, create a symlink called `current` that points to `releases/v1.2`.
Read a file through it: `cat current/app.conf`. Show where it points with `readlink current`.
Create a hard link `db-hard.conf` and a symlink `db-soft.conf`, both to `shared/db.conf`.
Show the link count with `stat -c '%n links=%h' shared/db.conf db-hard.conf`.
Delete `shared/db.conf`. Now `cat` both links. Which one still works?
Switch `current` to `releases/v1.1` with `ln -sfn`. Check with `cat current/app.conf`.
hints: `ln` makes a hard link. `ln -s` makes a symbolic link (symlink). The order is `ln -s TARGET LINK_NAME`.
A hard link is a second name for the same data. A symlink only stores a path to the target.
`ln -s releases/v1.2 current`, `ln shared/db.conf db-hard.conf`, `ln -s shared/db.conf db-soft.conf`, then `rm shared/db.conf`.

learn.title: Name -> inode -> data
text: A folder stores **names**. Each name points to an **inode**: a record with the owner, size, permissions and where the **data** is. The inode counts how many names point to it (the **link count**). The data is deleted only when that count is 0.

learn.title: Hard link vs symlink
art: db-soft.conf: a tiny file with the text "shared/db.conf"
└── Linux follows the path ──► shared/db.conf ──► inode 1234

learn.title: The `current` pointer
text: The web server always uses `current`. A deploy or a rollback only changes the link, in one step: `ln -sfn TARGET current` (`-s` symlink, `-f` replace, `-n` do not go inside the old link).

steps.say: Make the symlink `current` -> `releases/v1.2`. Target first, then the new name.
`stat -c %N` shows the link with an arrow, like `ls -l` does.
Use the link like a folder. `readlink` prints only the stored path.
Make a **hard** link (no `-s`) and a **symlink** (with `-s`) to `shared/db.conf`.
Ask for the file type of each name.
steps.code: stat -c '%n is a %F' shared/db.conf db-hard.conf db-soft.conf
steps.after: The hard link is a normal file name. The symlink is a different type.
steps.out:
shared/db.conf is a regular file
db-hard.conf is a regular file
db-soft.conf is a symbolic link

steps.say: Show the link count (`%h`).
steps.after: Both say 2: two names, one inode.

steps.say: Optional: `ls -li` shows the inode number first. Both names have the same number (the number differs on each machine).
Delete the "original" name.
Read both links. `||` runs the `echo` only if `cat` fails.
code: cat db-soft.conf || echo "db-soft.conf is a broken symlink"
steps.after: The hard link still has the data. The symlink's path leads to nothing.
steps.out:
db=todo
cat: db-soft.conf: No such file or directory
db-soft.conf is a broken symlink

steps.say: Roll back: point `current` to `v1.1` in one step.

explanation.meaning: Create a symlink called NAME that points to TARGET.
Print the path stored in the symlink.
Create a hard link: a second name for the same inode.
Number of hard links (names) the inode has.
Replace an existing symlink in one step. Common in deploy scripts.

problems.expected_output:
'current' -> 'releases/v1.2'
version=1.2
releases/v1.2
shared/db.conf is a regular file
db-hard.conf is a regular file
db-soft.conf is a symbolic link
shared/db.conf links=2
db-hard.conf links=2
db=todo
cat: db-soft.conf: No such file or directory
db-soft.conf is a broken symlink
'current' -> 'releases/v1.1'
version=1.1
mistakes: Wrong order: `ln -s current releases/v1.2` creates the link inside the target folder. The rule is `ln -s TARGET LINK`.

Running `ln -s releases/v1.1 current` when `current` already points to a folder gives no error, but it does not switch the link. It creates a new link inside the folder: `releases/v1.2/v1.1`. Use `ln -sfn`.
Hard link to a folder: `ln releases cur` gives `ln: releases: hard link not allowed for directory`.

checks.run: ln -s releases/v1.2 current; ln -s releases/v1.1 current; ls releases/v1.2

checks.expect: ln: releases: hard link not allowed for directory

problems.interview_say: A hard link is another name for the same inode, so it still works if the original name is deleted. A symlink stores a path, so it breaks when the target is removed, but it can point to folders and other disks. Deploy tools switch a `current` symlink with `ln -sfn`.
problems.try_yourself: Make a symlink with an absolute target: `ln -s ~/bash-practice/day01/links/releases/v1.2 abs-link`. Then `mv` both `abs-link` and `current` into another folder. Which one still works? Why?

problems.title: Find the bug: the log backup script
problems.situation: A teammate who usually works on Windows wrote `backup-logs.sh`. It prints "Backup done", but the backup folder is empty. **Goal:** read the error messages, find the 3 bugs, and fix the script.
outcomes: How to read a bash error message, and why the **first** error matters most.
Three common bugs: `mkdir` without `-p`, a Windows `\` in a path, `cp` of a folder.
How the glob `[1-5]` picks files.
spec: Make the folder `backup/2026-10` (and `backup`, if it is missing).
Copy only the logs from 1 to 5 October (`logs/app-2026-10-01.log` to `-05.log`) into it.
Copy every `.conf` file from `configs` into it.
When fixed, `backup/2026-10` has 7 files: 5 logs and 2 `.conf` files.
task: In `wild`, read the script with `cat backup-logs.sh`.
Run it: `bash backup-logs.sh`. Read every error line.
Find and fix 3 bugs (with `nano backup-logs.sh`).
Run it again and list `backup/2026-10`. You should see 5 logs and 2 conf files.
hints: Each error line points to one bug. Read them from the top.
Look at the folder separator, the missing parent folder, and copying a whole folder instead of files.
Use `mkdir -p`, change `\` to `/`, and use `configs/*.conf` instead of `configs`.

learn.title: Bash goes on after an error
text: Without `set -e`, a failed line prints an error and bash runs the next line. So the last line prints "Backup done" even when nothing was copied. Always check the result.

learn.title: How to read an error
art: mkdir: cannot create directory ‘backup/2026-10’: No such file or directory
program      what it tried                         why it failed
learn.after: Fix the **first** error first. Later errors are often caused by it.

learn.title: The three bug types

head: Bug
Why it breaks
Fix
rows: `\` escapes the next letter and disappears: `logsapp-...`

learn.after: `0[1-5]` matches `01` to `05`: `[1-5]` is **one** character from 1 to 5.

files.name: backup-logs.sh
files.say: The whole fixed file. Each part has a comment that says what it does and why.
content: #   1. Makes the folder backup/2026-10 (and the folder backup, if it is missing).
#   2. Copies the logs from 1 to 5 October into backup/2026-10.
#   3. Copies every .conf file from the configs folder into backup/2026-10.
# All paths below are relative (they do not start with /),
# so the script must be run from inside the wild folder.
# Without -p, mkdir fails, because the folder "backup" does not exist yet.
# With -p there is also no error if the folder already exists,
# so the script is safe to run again tomorrow.
# ---- Step 2: copy the October logs from day 01 to day 05 ----
# Linux paths use the forward slash /. (Windows uses the backslash \.)
# [1-5] matches ONE character from 1 to 5, so 0[1-5] matches 01 02 03 04 05,
# The / at the end of backup/2026-10/ means "copy the files INTO this folder".
# ---- Step 3: copy all .conf files (the files, not the folder) ----
# Bash changes configs/*.conf into: configs/api.conf configs/web.conf
# (Copying the folder "configs" itself would need cp -r.)
# ---- Step 4: say that the script reached the end ----
# Note: bash runs this line even if a command above failed.
# Problem 3 shows how set -e stops a script at the first error.

steps.say: Read the broken script first. Never run a script you have not read.
steps.out:
#!/bin/bash
# Copy October logs 01-05 and all .conf files into backup/2026-10
mkdir backup/2026-10
cp logs\app-2026-10-0[1-5].log backup/2026-10/
cp configs backup/2026-10/
echo "Backup done"

steps.say: Run it and read **every** error line from the top.
steps.after: Error 1 (line 3): `backup` does not exist. Error 2 (line 4): the `\` disappeared, so the path became `logsapp-...`. Error 3 (line 5): `configs` is a folder. Then "Backup done" is printed anyway.
steps.out:
mkdir: cannot create directory ‘backup/2026-10’: No such file or directory
cp: cannot stat 'logsapp-2026-10-0[1-5].log': No such file or directory
cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'configs'
Backup done

steps.say: Check the result. Do not trust "Backup done".
steps.out: ls: cannot access 'backup': No such file or directory

steps.say: Open the script and fix the 3 lines: `mkdir -p`, `/` instead of `\`, and `configs/*.conf`. Save with **Ctrl+O**, **Enter**, close with **Ctrl+X**.
Run the fixed script.
Check the result: 5 logs and 2 conf files.
steps.after: Days 06 to 09 were not copied, because `[1-5]` does not match them.
steps.out:
api.conf	    app-2026-10-02.log	app-2026-10-04.log  web.conf
app-2026-10-01.log  app-2026-10-03.log	app-2026-10-05.log

steps.say: Run it once more. A good script is safe to run again.

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: `backup` did not exist, so plain `mkdir` failed. Fix: `mkdir -p backup/2026-10` makes both levels.
Bug 2: the Windows backslash. In bash `\` escapes the next letter and disappears, so the path became `logsapp-...`. Fix: use `/`.
Bug 3: it copied the folder, not the files, and `cp` needs `-r` for a folder. Fix: `configs/*.conf` copies the files inside.

problems.expected_output:
#!/bin/bash
# Copy October logs 01-05 and all .conf files into backup/2026-10
mkdir backup/2026-10
cp logs\app-2026-10-0[1-5].log backup/2026-10/
cp configs backup/2026-10/
echo "Backup done"
mkdir: cannot create directory ‘backup/2026-10’: No such file or directory
cp: cannot stat 'logsapp-2026-10-0[1-5].log': No such file or directory
cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'configs'
Backup done
ls: cannot access 'backup': No such file or directory

api.conf	    app-2026-10-02.log	app-2026-10-04.log  web.conf

mistakes: Only fixing the last error. Always fix from the first error down; later errors are often caused by the first one.
Writing `cp configs/ backup/` and getting `cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'configs/'`.
Thinking "Backup done" means success. The script has no error checks, so it prints it anyway (`set -e` fixes this, see problem 3).
problems.interview_say: I read the first error first. Here the script used Windows backslashes, a `mkdir` without `-p`, and copied a folder without `-r`. I fixed the paths, used a glob for the files, and checked the result with `ls` instead of trusting the success message.
problems.try_yourself: Add `set -euo pipefail` as line 2 of the **broken** script and run it. How many error lines do you see now, and why?

problems.title: Wildcards: predict which files a pattern matches
problems.situation: Cleanup scripts delete files with patterns like `*.log`. A wrong pattern deletes the wrong files. **Goal:** guess what each pattern matches, then check, before using patterns with `rm`.
outcomes: `*`, `?` and `[ ]`, and that **bash** expands them before the command runs.
What happens when nothing matches.
Why braces `{ }` and quotes behave differently.
task: In `match`, look at the names with `ls`.
Before running, write down what each command prints: `echo api-?.log`, `echo api-*.log`, `echo api-[12].log`, `echo *.txt`, `echo *.yml`, `echo config-{dev,prod}.yml`.
Run them and compare with your guesses.
hints: `?` = exactly one character. `*` = any text (also empty).
`[12]` = one character, 1 or 2. If nothing matches, bash leaves the pattern as it is.
Braces `{}` do not look at files at all. They always expand.

learn.title: Bash expands the pattern first
art: bash looks at the folder, then runs:
learn.after: So `echo PATTERN` is a safe way to test a pattern before `rm`.

head: Pattern
Matches
Looks at files?
rows: one character from the list / range
makes the words, even if no file exists

learn.after: No match? Bash keeps the pattern as plain text: `echo *.yml` prints `*.yml`.

Guess first: `?` is exactly one character.

mistakes: Quoting the pattern: `echo "api-*.log"` prints `api-*.log`. Quotes stop wildcard expansion.
Expecting `?` to match `10`. It matches only one character.
problems.interview_say: Globs like `*`, `?` and `[ ]` are expanded by the shell to existing file names before the command runs. Braces just generate words. I test a pattern with `echo` or `ls` before I use it with `rm`.
problems.try_yourself: Run `shopt -s nullglob` and then `echo *.yml`. What changes? Run `shopt -u nullglob` to turn it off again.

problems.title: Inspect a file before opening it: ls -la, file, stat, zcat
problems.situation: Files copied from other servers often have no extension, and some are compressed. **Goal:** read every column of `ls -la`, find the real type of a file with `file`, and read a compressed log without unpacking it.
outcomes: The columns of `ls -la`.
Why Linux does not need extensions, and how `file` finds the real type.
`stat -c` for exact details, and `zcat` for `.gz` logs.
task: In `inspect`, run `ls -la` and read each column.
Run `file *` to see the real type of each file.
Show name, size in bytes and permissions with `stat -c '%n %s bytes %A' *`.
Read the compressed file without unpacking it: `zcat old-logs`.
hints: Linux does not need extensions. `file` looks inside the file.
`stat -c` with `%s` gives size in bytes and `%A` gives permissions like `-rwxr-xr-x`.
`*` does not match hidden files, so `.env` is not in the `file *` output.

learn.title: One line of ls -la
art: type: - file, d folder, l symlink

learn.title: The real type of a file
text: On Linux a name is only a name; `deploy` can be a script with no extension. `file` reads the first bytes and tells the real type. `zcat` prints a gzip file without unpacking it (`zgrep` searches it).

mistakes: Running `cat old-logs` on a gzip file prints strange symbols. Use `file` first, then `zcat`.

problems.interview_say: Linux does not depend on file extensions. I use `file` to see the real type and `stat` for exact size, owner and times. For rotated logs I use `zcat` or `zgrep` without unpacking them.

cards.q: Which command prints the folder you are in now?
cards.what: **p**rint **w**orking **d**irectory.
cards.does: Prints the full (absolute) path of the current folder.
flags: show the real path, with symlinks resolved

cards.q: How do you go back to the folder you were in before?
cards.what: `cd` changes the current folder. `-` means the previous folder.
cards.does: Jumps back and prints the folder name.

cards.q: Which command shows hidden files too?
cards.what: `ls` lists a folder. Hidden files have names that start with a dot.
cards.does: `-a` shows **a**ll files, also `.env`, `.` and `..`.
flags: long list: type, permissions, owner, size, date

cards.q: Which folder holds the config files of the system?
cards.what: The settings folder.
cards.does: Examples: `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`, `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`.

cards.q: Which folder holds the log files?
cards.what: `var` = variable data that changes; logs grow all the time.
cards.does: Examples: `/var/log/syslog`, `/var/log/nginx/error.log`.

cards.q: What is the home folder of the root user?
cards.what: `root` is the admin user.
cards.does: Not the same as `/`, the root directory at the top of the tree.

cards.q: Which command shows where a command's program file is?
cards.what: A bash built-in that prints what bash will run for a name.
cards.does: Prints the path, for example `/usr/bin/ls`.
flags: also says if it is an alias or a built-in

cards.q: How do you make a folder and all its missing parent folders?
cards.what: **m**a**k**e **dir**ectory, with **p**arents.
cards.does: Makes every missing level. No error if the folder already exists, so it is safe in scripts.
flags: make parents; no error if it exists

cards.q: How do you copy a whole folder with everything inside?
cards.what: `cp` copies. Folders need `-r` (recursive).
cards.does: Copies the folder and all levels inside it. The order is always: from, then to.
flags: archive: like -r, and keeps owner, permissions and times (good for backups)

cards.q: Which command renames a file?
cards.what: **m**o**v**e. Moving to a new name in the same folder is a rename.
cards.does: Moves or renames files and folders. It replaces an existing target without asking.

cards.q: How do you delete a folder and everything in it?
cards.what: **r**e**m**ove, **r**ecursive.
cards.does: Deletes for ever. There is no recycle bin. Check the path with `ls` first.

cards.q: Make a symlink called `current` that points to `releases/v1.2`.
cards.what: A **symlink** is a small file that stores a path, like a shortcut.
cards.does: Order: TARGET first, then the new NAME.
flags: symbolic link (without it: a hard link)
do not go inside a link to a folder
switch a release link in one step

cards.q: Which command prints where a symlink points?
cards.what: Reads the path stored inside a symlink.
cards.does: `readlink current` prints `releases/v1.2`.
flags: full absolute path, following every link

cards.q: Which link still works after the original file is deleted?
cards.what: A hard link is a second name for the same inode (the file record).
cards.does: The data stays until the last name is deleted. A symlink only stores a path, so it breaks.

cards.q: Which command tells the real type of a file, not by its name?
cards.what: Reads the first bytes of the file.
cards.does: Says for example `gzip compressed data` or `Bourne-Again shell script`.

cards.q: How do you print only chosen details of a file (size, owner, link count)?
cards.what: `stat` shows file details; `-c` takes a format.
cards.does: Prints only the fields in the format.

cards.q: How do you read a `.gz` log without unpacking it?
cards.what: `cat` for gzip files.
cards.does: Unpacks in memory and prints the text. The file on disk stays compressed.

cards.q: Which wildcard matches exactly one character?
cards.what: A wildcard (glob) is a pattern for file names. Bash expands it before the command runs.
cards.does: `api-?.log` matches `api-1.log` but not `api-10.log`.
flags: braces: make words, not a wildcard

cards.q: What is the first line of a bash script called, and what is it?
cards.what: The **shebang**.
cards.does: Tells Linux which program runs the file when it is started with `./script.sh`.

cards.q: Which line makes a script stop at the first error?
cards.what: Safety options for bash scripts. Put it right after the shebang.
cards.does: Stops the script instead of going on with broken data.
flags: error on a variable that is not set
a pipe fails if any part fails

cards.q: How do you make a script executable and run it from the current folder?
cards.what: `chmod +x` adds the execute permission. `./` means "this folder".
cards.does: Without `+x` the user gets `Permission denied`. `bash script.sh` works without it.

interview.q: What is the difference between an absolute path and a relative path?
interview.a: An absolute path starts at the root directory `/`, for example `/var/log/nginx`. It works from any folder. A relative path starts from the current folder, for example `logs/app.log`.

interview.q: What is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link?
interview.a: A hard link is a second name for the same data, so it still works if the original is deleted. A symlink stores a path. It breaks when the target is deleted, but it can point to folders and to other disks.

interview.q: Where are config files and log files kept in Linux?
interview.a: Config files are in `/etc`, for example `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`. Logs are in `/var/log`, for example `/var/log/syslog`.

interview.q: How do you see hidden files? What makes a file hidden?
interview.a: A file is hidden when its name starts with a dot, like `.env`. `ls -a` or `ls -la` shows hidden files.
`-r` deletes folders with everything inside and `-f` never asks and hides errors. There is no recycle bin. With a wrong or empty variable it can delete the wrong folder.
